content:
For odd \(a\), if \(p\) is odd then \(p^2+a\) is even and \(>2\), so composite. Thus \(p=2\), and similarly \(q=2\), contradicting distinctness. So no odd \(a\) works.

For even \(a\), \(p=2\) gives \(p^2+a\) even and \(>2\), so \(p,q\) must be odd primes.

If \(a\equiv 2\pmod 3\) (here \(a=2,8\)), then for any odd prime \(p\neq 3\), \(p^2+a\equiv 1+2\equiv 0\pmod 3\) and is \(>3\), so composite. Hence \(p=q=3\), not distinct. Thus \(a=2,8\) fail.

For the remaining even \(a\):
- \(a=4\): \(p=3,q=5\) gives \(13,29\), all distinct primes.
- \(a=6\): \(p=5,q=11\) gives \(31,127\), all distinct primes.
- \(a=10\): \(p=3,q=7\) gives \(19,59\), all distinct primes.

Thus the valid \(a\)'s are \(4,6,10\), and their sum is

\[
4+6+10=\boxed{20}.
\]
